sec.t:
In the Arab world, cooks have long made *luqmat al-qadi*, which means "the judge's morsels". These are small fried balls of [[yeast|yeast]] dough, drenched in honey or syrup. They appear in cookbooks from Baghdad written around 800 years ago. Persians made similar sweets.

Persian-speaking traders, soldiers and rulers brought many foods and words to India. Under the Delhi Sultanate and later the [[@mughals|Mughals]], Persian was the language of royal courts. It is likely that the idea of a fried, syrup-soaked ball met Indian milk sweets somewhere along the way. A popular story says a cook of Emperor Shah Jahan invented gulab jamun by accident. It is a fun tale, but there is no written proof.

India has a whole family of gulab jamun relatives. *Kala jamun* is fried longer until it is almost black. Bengal has *pantua*, made partly with chhena, a fresh cheese. One famous Bengal version is called *ledikeni*. The story goes that a Kolkata sweet maker created it in the 1850s to honour Lady Canning, the wife of the governor-general, and people mispronounced her name.

In Rajasthan, some cooks go further. *Gulab jamun ki sabzi* is a curry where the sweets go into a spicy tomato and onion gravy, so every bite is sweet, salty and hot together. It sounds strange, but plenty of Rajasthani families swear by it, and cooking videos of it get curious viewers from all over India.

Gulab jamun turns up at weddings, birthdays and festivals like Diwali and Eid. Shops in India sell it from huge steel pots, and tins of it are shipped to Indian grocery stores across the USA, the UK and the Gulf.

It is very sweet, and a single gulab jamun can carry about as much [[@sugar|sugar]] as two or three teaspoons, so most families save it for special days. The same syrup trick appears in another favourite, the crunchy spiral [[@food-jalebi|jalebi]], which also has cousins across the Middle East. And at the heart of both lies one of India's oldest skills, turning plain [[@milk|milk]] into dozens of sweets.

text: Jaggery, called gur in Hindi, is a traditional sweetener made by boiling sugarcane juice until it turns thick, sticky and golden-brown. It is then poured into moulds and left to set into blocks or cones. In some regions, especially Bengal and Tamil Nadu, jaggery is also made from the sap of date or palmyra palms.

Unlike white sugar, jaggery isn't refined. It keeps the brown [[@oddity-great-molasses-flood|molasses]] and a little of the minerals from the cane. That gives it a rich, caramel-like taste. India makes most of the world's jaggery and uses it in [[@candy-history|sweets]], dals, drinks and [[@festival-foods|festival foods]].

st.prompt: Jaggery is brown, while white sugar is white. What makes the difference?

options.t: Jaggery keeps the molasses that white sugar has removed
Jaggery is made from a different, brown kind of sugarcane
Jaggery is burnt sugar

st.reveal: Jaggery is simply cane juice boiled down until it sets, so it keeps the dark, sticky molasses and small amounts of minerals. To make white sugar, factories spin and wash out the molasses, leaving pure white crystals.

sec.t:
In the winter harvest season, sugarcane is cut and taken to small workshops called kolhus or gur-making units. There, crushers squeeze out the juice.

The juice is poured into huge, shallow iron pans over a fire. As it [[@boiling-water|boils]], water evaporates and the juice thickens. Workers skim off the scum that rises to the top, sometimes adding plant extracts to help clean it. After a few hours, the thick, golden liquid is stirred, cooled and poured into moulds.

The whole process is simple and has changed little in centuries, though many units now use better furnaces. Kolhapur in Maharashtra is especially famous for its jaggery, and its market yard trades huge amounts every season.

In Bengal, a special winter jaggery called nolen gur is made from the sap of date palms. Tappers climb the trees in the cold early morning to collect the sap. Nolen gur has a smoky, fragrant taste and goes into Bengali sweets like sandesh and [[@bengali-food|rosogolla]].

In Tamil Nadu and Kerala, palmyra palms give karupatti, a darker palm jaggery with a deep, earthy flavour.

Jaggery is part of many celebrations. On Makar Sankranti in Maharashtra, people exchange tilgul, sweets made of sesame seeds and jaggery. In Tamil Nadu, sweet pongal is made with new rice, moong dal and jaggery during the harvest festival of [[@onam-pongal|Pongal]].

Chikki, a crunchy sweet of [[@peanut-butter|peanuts]] and jaggery, is famous in Lonavala in Maharashtra. Many families also add a small piece of jaggery to dal, especially in Gujarat and Maharashtra, for a sweet-sour taste.

Many people think jaggery is much healthier than white sugar. It does contain small amounts of iron, potassium and magnesium, which white sugar lacks. But it's still around 80 per cent or more sugar.

Too much of any sugar can cause [[@tooth-decay|tooth decay]] and other health problems. The [[bacteria|bacteria]] in your mouth don't care whether the [[@sugar-teeth|sugar]] came from a factory or a village pan. Jaggery's taste and traditions are good reasons to enjoy it, but it's still a treat, not a health food. Sweet things, in any form, are best eaten in small amounts.
